subject: Copywriting
title: The Negative Slogan
description: A 60-second lesson on The Negative Slogan.

hook.text: 'Don't Be Evil' was Google's motto. 'Impossible Is Nothing' denies limitation.

buildup.text: Negative slogans stand out because most advertising is relentlessly positive. The contrast makes them memorable.

discovery.text: Avis's 'We Try Harder' implied Hertz didn't try. The negative comparison was embedded in the positive claim.

twist.text: Google dropped 'Don't Be Evil' as its official motto in 2015. The slogan became a weapon critics used against them.

climax.text: Negative slogans are double-edged. They're memorable but provide ammunition. 'Don't be evil' invites 'But you are.'

punchline.text: Negatives grab attention. But they give critics a weapon too.

quiz.question: Why did Google drop 'Don't Be Evil'?
options: Critics used it as ammunition against the company
It was trademarked by someone else

details.summary: Negative slogans use negation to make a positive point. Adidas's 'Impossible Is Nothing' and Apple's 'Think Different' both use words associated with limitation to convey liberation. The contradiction creates cognitive tension that demands attention and resolution.
details.whyItMatters: Negative framing stands out in a sea of positive affirmations. Understanding how negation creates impact helps writers craft slogans that challenge expectations.
takeaways: Negative words in slogans create surprise and cognitive engagement
Contradiction between word and meaning produces memorable tension
The best negative slogans reframe limitations as possibilities

faq.question: Why do negative words sometimes make better slogans?
faq.answer: Negative words violate expectations in a landscape of relentless positivity. The brain pays more attention to unexpected stimuli. By claiming 'impossible is nothing,' Adidas forces the reader to mentally wrestle with the paradox, deepening engagement.

faq.question: Are there risks to using negative language in slogans?
faq.answer: Yes — research shows people sometimes remember only the negative word, stripping away context. A slogan like 'Nothing is impossible' could be misremembered as 'Nothing is possible.' Careful testing ensures the intended meaning survives memory compression.
